6 Rs framework: How would you decide bet: Assess each application on business value versus technical debt/complexity: rehost (lift-and-shift) for low-complexity, time-pressured migrations where cloud-native benefits aren't the priority yet; replatform for moderate effort with some cloud optimization (e.g. moving to a managed database) without a full rewrite; refactor/re-architect for high-value applications where cloud-native scalability/cost benefits justify the investment; repurchase when a SaaS alternative genuinely replaces the need for the custom application; retire for genuinely unused or redundant applications discovered during portfolio assessment; and retain for applications with a hard blocker (regulatory, a dependency that can't move) that must stay on-prem for now. This assessment should be done application-by-application, not as a blanket policy for the whole portfolio.
Migration wave planning: How would you s: Map the full dependency graph first (which applications call which), then sequence waves so that applications a wave depends on have already migrated (or have a working hybrid-connectivity bridge back to on-prem) before that wave moves - moving a dependent application before its dependency creates unnecessary cross-environment latency and complexity mid-migration. Start with lower-risk, standalone or edge applications to build team confidence and validate the migration process itself, saving the most business-critical, highly-interdependent core systems for later waves once the process is proven and any tooling/runbook gaps have already been found on lower-stakes applications.
Data migration validation: How would you: Validate at multiple levels: row/object counts matching between source and destination, checksums or hash comparisons on a sample (or all, for critical data) of records/files to confirm byte-level integrity, and application-level validation (running representative queries/workflows against the migrated data and comparing results to the source system). For ongoing replication tools (like Database Migration Service's continuous replication), monitor replication lag and confirm it reaches zero before cutover, and run this validation more than once - a single point-in-time check can miss data that changed on the source after validation but before actual cutover.
Cutover and rollback: How would you plan: Plan cutover during the lowest-traffic window with a defined, tested runbook (not improvised), using a DNS-based or load-balancer-based traffic shift that can be reversed quickly (short TTLs set well in advance of cutover, so a DNS rollback actually propagates fast when needed). The rollback plan must be prepared and tested beforehand, not designed after something goes wrong - define clear rollback trigger criteria (specific error rate/latency thresholds that mean 'abort and revert') decided in advance, since deciding rollback criteria live during a stressful cutover leads to worse decisions than deciding calmly ahead of time.
Cost and TCO estimation: How would you e: Estimate using actual historical utilization data (not theoretical peak capacity) mapped to equivalent cloud resource pricing, including often-underestimated costs: data egress/transfer costs (especially recurring cross-cloud or hybrid traffic), the cost of running in a non-optimized 'lift-and-shift' state before right-sizing, licensing cost changes (some software licensing models don't map cleanly to cloud consumption pricing), and the ongoing operational cost of any new tooling/platform team needed to run the cloud environment. Validate post-migration by comparing actual billing data against the pre-migration estimate after a full billing cycle or two, adjusting future estimates based on where the initial estimate was wrong.
Migrate for Compute Engine: When would y: Use Migrate for Compute Engine when speed of migration matters more than immediate cloud-native optimization (a hard deadline like a data center exit), or for applications not easily containerized/re-architected in the migration timeframe - it gets workloads off the source platform quickly as VMs, with re-architecture as a deliberate later phase. Rebuild directly on GKE/Cloud Run when the application is already containerized or straightforward to containerize, and when the migration timeline allows investing in the cloud-native benefits (autoscaling, managed operations) immediately rather than migrating twice (once to VMs, then again to managed services later).
Hybrid connectivity during migration: Ho: Establish a Dedicated/Partner Interconnect or Cloud VPN for reliable, low-latency connectivity between on-prem and the VPC, with routes configured so on-prem and cloud components can reach each other as if on the same network during the transition period. For identity, federate the existing on-prem identity provider (Active Directory) with Cloud Identity/IAM so users and service accounts have consistent access across both environments without maintaining two separate identity systems during the split-state period, which is critical since a phased migration can last months and inconsistent identity across environments creates both security risk and operational friction.
Scenario: Post-migration, a newly migrat: Isolate layer by layer: check network path/latency first (a different region choice, or hybrid connectivity still routing some calls back on-prem unexpectedly, can add real latency), compare actual provisioned compute sizing against the source platform's (a 'lift and shift' sometimes under-provisions relative to what the source environment quietly had), check storage IOPS/throughput limits (a different disk type/tier than the source can be a silent bottleneck, especially for I/O-heavy workloads), and check application configuration for anything environment-specific that didn't carry over correctly (connection pool sizes, timeout values tuned for the old environment's characteristics). Use distributed tracing if available to see exactly where the extra latency accumulates within a request rather than guessing across all four possibilities simultaneously.
Scenario: A client wants to migrate a pr: Map services directly: GKE workloads to EKS (largely portable since both are standard Kubernetes, though node/networking configuration differs), Cloud SQL to RDS (schema/data migration via a database migration tool, or native export/import for smaller datasets), Cloud Storage to S3 (bulk transfer via a tool like `rclone` or AWS's Storage Gateway/DataSync), and re-implement IAM policies in AWS IAM's equivalent model (the concepts map but the policy syntax/structure differs significantly, so this needs to be rebuilt rather than directly copied). Plan data transfer with validation checksums, cut over DNS with pre-shortened TTLs for fast reversibility, and keep the GCP environment running unchanged as the rollback target until the AWS environment has proven stable in production for a defined soak period.

Map EKS workloads to GKE (Kubernetes manifests are largely portable; cloud-specific parts like ingress annotations, storage classes, and IAM/Workload Identity integration need rework), RDS to Cloud SQL (via Database Migration Service for supported engines, handling schema and data with minimal downtime through continuous replication until cutover), S3 to Cloud Storage (Storage Transfer Service handles large-scale bucket-to-bucket migration natively, including ongoing sync during a phased cutover), and rebuild IAM policies in GCP's IAM model rather than attempting a direct policy translation. Validate data integrity before cutover, use a DNS-based cutover with pre-shortened TTLs, and retain the AWS environment as a tested rollback target for a defined period post-cutover.
Scenario: A client wants to migrate a wo: Map AKS to GKE (Kubernetes manifests largely portable, Azure-specific ingress/storage integrations need rework), Azure SQL to Cloud SQL (schema/data migration, checking for any Azure SQL-specific features/extensions that don't have a direct GCP equivalent), Blob Storage to Cloud Storage (via Storage Transfer Service, which has native support for Azure Blob as a source), and Azure AD to Cloud Identity/Google Workspace (via identity federation, since a full Azure AD replacement isn't usually the goal - federating lets on-prem/Azure AD identities authenticate into GCP resources during and after migration). For networking, VNet-to-VPC migration requires re-mapping CIDR ranges and firewall/NSG rules to GCP's VPC firewall model (conceptually similar but syntactically and structurally different), and watch closely for identity federation edge cases (group membership sync timing, conditional access policies that don't have a direct GCP IAM equivalent) that can cause access issues during the transition.

Map AKS to EKS (Kubernetes manifests portable with rework needed for Azure-specific ingress/storage class integrations), Azure SQL to RDS (schema/data migration via AWS Database Migration Service, checking for Azure SQL-specific feature usage that needs a workaround on RDS), Blob Storage to S3 (via AWS DataSync or a third-party tool supporting Azure Blob as a source), and Azure AD to AWS IAM Identity Center federated with the existing Azure AD (rather than a full identity system replacement, federation is typically the practical migration path). For networking, VNet-to-VPC migration requires re-mapping address ranges and translating NSG rules into AWS security groups/NACLs (different enforcement model - security groups are stateful and instance-level, NACLs are stateless and subnet-level), and watch for identity federation timing issues (group sync delays, conditional access policy gaps) causing access problems during the transition window.
